newsitem.title: USA: Maker of Zig-Zag papers to sell junk bonds.
newsitem.headline: Maker of Zig-Zag papers to sell junk bonds.

text.p: Holy smokes! Investors looking to satisfy their craving for junk bonds will have a chance to buy a new issue from a company whose main products will be Beech-Nut chewing tobacco and Zig-Zag rolling papers.

National Tobacco Co. LP, the nation's third-largest maker of chewing tobacco, is buying North Atlantic Trading Co., the biggest maker of "roll-your-own" cigarette papers, and the new company plans to raise $115 million by selling high-yield bonds to finance the deal and refinance existing debt.
The closely held companies will use the North Atlantic Trading name after the merger. The new company will be based in New York.
Underwriters NatWest Securities Corp. and CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. are expected to sell the seven-year bonds to institutional investors Thursday.

The bonds are expected to yield 11 percent to 11.25 percent, about 4.5 percentage points above comparable Treasury bonds. The bonds are ranked below investment-grade and considered highly speculative by Standard & Poor's and Moody's Investors Service, two major bond rating agencies.
Underwriters acknowledged the risk of investing in a tobacco products company, as the industry is under attack from anti-smoking forces.
Investment banking officials admitted that smokeless tobacco companies may have to bear part of the burden of any settlement between the industry and anti-smoking forces.
But the officials, who asked not to be quoted by name, said settlement costs probably would be small enough for the new company to pass on to consumers without putting a big dent in sales.
Company officials did not return phone calls.

The bankers noted that National Tobacco has never lost or settled a lawsuit alleging that using chewing tobacco causes disease. Moreover, like cigarette making, the chewing tobacco and rolling paper businesses were very lucrative, they said.
Both Beech-Nut chewing tobacco and Zig-Zag rolling papers generate big profits and have extremely loyal customers, they noted.
Moody's said chewing tobacco sales were shrinking 2 percent a year but that National Tobacco has expanded its business by developing new products aimed at niche customers.

Investors have become more wary about tobacco company securities since news of the settlement talks emerged in April. But the talks showed signs of fraying on Tuesday, state officials and other negotiators said in Washington.

Sources close to the National Tobacco-North Atlantic deal said Wall Street's wariness about tobacco investments might actually help make the bonds more attractive. If only a few investors bid for the bonds, that could drive yields higher.

"There are some accounts that have restrictions on investments in tobacco-related companies. So investors in this deal could get paid a premium given the fact that this is tobacco company," one market source said.
